To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the two human monoclonals, anti-TT1 (IgG1) and anti-TT-2 (IgG2), bind to distinct sites of the TToxin molecule, that the combination of the antibodies shows a synergistic neutralizing effect in vitro, and that mice are completely protected against a lethal challenge with TToxin by a combination of the two reagents.
the two monoclonal antibodies, anti-TT1 (IgG1 kappa, kappa light chain) and anti-TT 2 (IgG 1 kappa, kappa chain), bind to the B-fragment and C-fragment, respectively, of TToxin.

the combination of two human MAbs, one binding to the heavy chain and the second one to the light chain of the toxin molecule, is superior in neutralization of the tetanus toxin than either reagent used alone.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the generation and characterization of human monoclonal B-cell hybrids specific for tetanus toxoid and tetanus toxin.
the generation of human monoclonal antibody-producing hybridomas and with the application of these hybridomas for the production of monoclonal antibodies for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.
the production of human monoclonal anti-TToxin antibodies and their application for the protection of mice against TToxin.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

human monoclonal antibody production is feasible in the human-human fusion system and that the human-human fusion technology may be a promising approach for the development of human monoclonal reagents for diagnostic and/or therapeutic purposes.
human monoclonal antibody production is feasible, and that the production of human monoclonal anti-tetanus antibodies is possible.
human monoclonal antibody technology has reached a level of sophistication that allows its use in the development of human monoclonal reagents for therapeutic purposes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the human B-lymphocyte fusion technique can be used to generate human monoclonal antibody reagents for the therapy of human disease.

human monoclonal antibody technology has reached a stage where the production of human antibodies against any antigen is feasible and where the use of these antibodies as therapeutic agents is possible.
the combination of two antibodies recognizing distinct epitope regions on the TToxin molecule was superior to either of them alone in the protection of mice against the toxin.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combination of human monoclonal IgG1 antibodies against distinct epitopes on TToxin resulted in a synergistic neutralization of the toxin in mice.

the combination of two monoclonal antibodies against distinct epitopes on TToxin can provide complete protection of mice against TToxin challenge, while either monoclonal antibody alone only results in a delay of the death of the mice.
the use of two monoclonal antibodies that recognize distinct epitopes can be a more effective approach for neutralization of toxins than the use of single reagents.
